title: India and China Reopen Himalayan Border Trade After Six-Year Freeze
excerpt: Trade through three high-altitude passes — Lipulekh, Shipki La, and Nathu La — resumes for the first time since 2019, with transactions shifting from barter to rupee-yuan currency exchange.
body:
• India and China have reopened border trade through three Himalayan passes — Lipulekh (Uttarakhand), Shipki La (Himachal Pradesh), and Nathu La (Sikkim) — after a six-year suspension caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2020 Galwan Valley standoff.
  • Trade will now be conducted in Indian Rupees and Chinese Yuan, replacing the centuries-old barter system, and will be fully road-based for the first time across all three routes.
  • Nepal has formally objected to the Lipulekh Pass trade route, claiming the territory — including Kalapani and Limpiyadhura — lies within its borders.

Ancient Trade Routes Reawaken

After six years of silence along some of the world's highest trade corridors, India and China have reopened border commerce through three Himalayan passes, marking one of the most tangible signs of warming bilateral ties since the deadly Galwan Valley clashes of 2020.

https://x.com/ANI/status/2083515067652604346

Trade through Shipki La Pass in Himachal Pradesh's Kinnaur district commenced on June 1, 2026, kicking off a six-month season that runs until November 30. The Lipulekh Pass in Uttarakhand's Pithoragarh district followed, with its traditional June-to-September trade window, after the Ministry of External Affairs issued a No-Objection Certificate. Nathu La in Sikkim, where infrastructure restoration along the historic route has been completed, is also set to resume operations.

The reopening was agreed upon during the 24th round of Special Representatives' talks between National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi during Wang's two-day visit to India in August 2025. At those talks, the two sides also agreed to restore direct flight connectivity.

From Barter to Currency: A Historic Shift

Perhaps the most significant change is structural. For the first time, cross-border trade through all three passes will be conducted in Indian Rupees and Chinese Yuan, replacing a barter system that dates back centuries. Traders historically exchanged goods directly — Tibetan merchants bringing salt, borax, animal products, and medicinal herbs across the passes, while Indian traders carried goats, sheep, grains, spices, jaggery, and wheat in the other direction.

The shift to currency-based trade required new banking infrastructure. In Uttarakhand, the Customs Department and Dharchula administration have prepared detailed plans for designated bank branches handling currency exchange, while customs workshops and security verification are underway at Shipki La.

"Trade had been stopped for five years, and many bills remained pending on both sides. The reopening brings hope for us."

— Anil Gupta, trader, Gangtok

Under the existing framework at Shipki La, approved traders can import 20 designated items and export 36 approved goods. Sikkim-based traders have urged authorities to update the tradable goods list established in 2006, requesting the inclusion of commodities like sugar and matchsticks that are in high demand across the border.

Why It Took Six Years

Border trade through these routes was last active in 2019. The COVID-19 pandemic initially suspended operations, but the June 2020 Galwan Valley clash — which killed 20 Indian soldiers and an undetermined number of Chinese troops — froze all cooperation along the Line of Actual Control for years.

The diplomatic thaw began in late 2024, when both sides agreed to disengage at remaining friction points along the LAC. The trade resumption, alongside the restart of the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra through Nathu La, signals a broader normalization that goes beyond military disengagement.

Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri's letter to Uttarakhand Chief Secretary Anand Bardhan confirmed that both the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Ministry of Commerce and Industry had cleared the trade resumption. Pithoragarh District Magistrate Ashish Bhatgai said preparations included issuing trade passes, deploying customs officials, and arranging transit camps, communication networks, security, and medical facilities for traders.

Nepal's Objection

The resumption has not been without friction. Nepal has formally protested the Lipulekh Pass trade route, asserting that Lipulekh, Kalapani, and Limpiyadhura lie within Nepali territory. Kathmandu has called on both India and China to halt activities in the disputed area.

Tensions over the route deepened in 2020 after India inaugurated a new road link to Kailash Mansarovar via Lipulekh, prompting Nepal to redraw its political map. China's position has generally aligned with India on the Lipulekh question — its 2023 official map placed the disputed area within Indian territory.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, the trade reopening carries significance beyond the modest volumes of traditional goods crossing the passes. It is a barometer of the India-China relationship — a dynamic that affects everything from global tech supply chains to geopolitical alignments that shape diaspora communities worldwide.

The shift from barter to currency-based trade also signals India's intent to formalize and modernize these ancient economic corridors. Jeevan Singh Ronkali, president of the Pithoragarh Border Trade Organisation, noted that traders will finally be able to retrieve goods stored in warehouses in Tibet's Taklakot since the 2019 suspension — a practical reminder that the freeze imposed real costs on border communities.

What's Next

Sikkim Commerce Minister T.T. Bhutia has urged the Centre to create a dedicated export promotion framework for Himalayan and northeastern states, focusing on export readiness, branding, logistics, and quality certification. At the 5th Board of Trade meeting in July 2026, he highlighted Sikkim's strengths in organic agriculture, pharmaceuticals, GI-tagged products, and wellness goods.

With the Shipki La season running through November and Lipulekh trade active through September, the coming months will test whether the reopening translates into meaningful economic activity — or remains largely symbolic. Traders on both sides of the border are watching closely.
